clue.text: Ups and downs expected when errand boys do a swap ?

definitions.text: Ups and downs expected when errand boys do a swap ?

parts.words: Ups and downs expected when errand boys do a swap
parts.note: errand boys swapping their bicycles would be trading cycles; read the other way it is the economic boom-and-bust pattern

explanation.surface: Delivery lads exchanging bikes are warned to expect a bumpy ride.
explanation.walkthrough: Errand boys rode delivery bicycles, so their swap is a trade of cycles; the phrase is also the economists' name for recurring booms and slumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Economists call the regular rise and fall of business activity by this name, so 'ups and downs' describes it.

clue.text: Invitation to the dance and response, words and music

parts.note: 'trip' as a command means dance nimbly, an invitation to step out
the eager reply 'let's!' accepts the invitation

explanation.surface: A partner is asked to dance and agrees, with a poem and a tune to go with it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition covers both arts: in verse three rhyming lines, in music three notes played in the time of two.
explanation.definitionFit: Groups of three occur both in poetry (three rhyming lines) and in music (three notes in the time of two).

clue.text: They are seen to exist only microscopically

definitions.text: They are seen to exist only microscopically

parts.words: They are seen to exist only microscopically
parts.note: the clue describes tiny creatures visible only under a microscope

explanation.surface: Something that can be seen only under a lens.
explanation.definitionFit: These are minute organisms, too small to see with the naked eye, so they show up only under magnification.

definitions.meaning: the stoat turns white in winter, and its winter fur has this name
robes trimmed with this white fur mark the dignity of judges and peers

explanation.walkthrough: The fur trims the robes of judges and peers in Britain, hence the sense of dignity.
explanation.definitionFit: The stoat's white winter fur trims ceremonial robes, so it stands for high rank and dignity.

parts.note: a good crop is a bumper output, and what pressure groups hope to win is that their opponents give way

explanation.surface: Campaigners count the fruits of their lobbying.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means a crop's output and also giving way under pressure, which is what pressure groups want.
explanation.definitionFit: A farm's output is its crop, and to give way under pressure is to give in; the word covers both.

parts.note: the Latin root lucubrare means to work by lamp at night

explanation.surface: A scholar working late at night under a lamp.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to work or write laboriously, especially at night by artificial light.

clue.text: There's a pungency about the old German doing railway work

indicators.note: the pungency is placed around the German, so its letters go on the outside

parts.note: a sharp smarting is a sting
Hun is an old disparaging nickname for a German

explanation.surface: An old German railwayman gives off a sharp smell as he works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hun' was a wartime slang name for a German; 'pungency' looks like the definition but supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving rolling stock between tracks in a yard is the railway task this word names.

definitions.meaning: a taxi is a form of hired transport
the Citizens Advice Bureau, abbreviated, gives free advice

explanation.walkthrough: The Citizens Advice Bureau is a British charity giving free advice, known by its initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi carries passengers, and the Citizens Advice Bureau, known by its initials, gives advice.

parts.note: the whip with nine tails is no laughing matter, and an animal that seldom grins is also hinted at

explanation.surface: Someone who rarely laughs.
explanation.walkthrough: The cat-o'-nine-tails was a flogging whip, no laughing matter; only the Cheshire one grins.
explanation.definitionFit: The feline seldom shows amusement, unlike the grinning one in Alice; the whip of that name was no laughing matter.

clue.text: "Mad, bad, and dangerous to know." Lord !

definitions.text: "Mad, bad, and dangerous to know." Lord !

parts.words: "Mad, bad, and dangerous to know." Lord
parts.note: Lady Caroline Lamb wrote these words about the Romantic poet who was a peer

explanation.surface: A famous description of a notorious aristocrat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Caroline Lamb described the Romantic poet-peer with these words after their affair.

indicators.note: the flower loses its leading letter

parts.note: lilium is the botanical name for the lily

explanation.surface: A girl called Lily loses her head in some place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' points to Troy, whose Latin name this is, where Helen lost her head over Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the Latin name for Troy, the place being pointed to, where Helen lost her head.
The word means both to come across someone and a fight between opposing forces.

clue.text: Nonsense man, Edward so well versed!

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse
Ned is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward Lear, the nonsense poet, was clearly well read in verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Lear wrote 'The Owl and the Pussycat'; 'versed' suits the poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Being scholarly or knowledgeable is to be well versed in a subject.

clue.text: West country hairdo? Not Sally Lunn's

parts.note: Bath is a city in the West Country of England
a bun is hair coiled at the back of the head

explanation.surface: A hairstyle from the West Country, not one belonging to a woman called Sally Lunn.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a city in South-West England; the Sally Lunn is another Bath teacake, so the definition says which Bath bake this is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sweet baked rolls from Bath, so the other famous Bath teacake is defined by contrast.

clue.text: It's the ruination of park bunting

definitions.text: It's the ruination of park bunting

indicators.note: ruining the words breaks them up so their letters can be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that wrecks the flags decorating a park.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruining someone financially leaves them insolvent, and the anagram itself ruins the park bunting.

definitions.meaning: a check mark against correct work
the click of a clock marking each second

explanation.definitionFit: A check mark rewards right answers, and a clock's click is a single beat of time.

parts.note: holding on to something, with a nod to the fee paid to secure a barrister's services

explanation.surface: Someone holding on to money they owe.
explanation.walkthrough: A barrister is engaged with a fee called a retainer, so the fee is named after this sense of keeping.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding something back is keeping it, and the fee that books a lawyer is called a retainer.

parts.note: the Latin root vocare means to call, so calling up memories is its sense rather than military service

explanation.surface: A question about conscription.
explanation.walkthrough: 'call-up' suggests military service, but the adjective describes calling up feelings or memories.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that summons up memories or feelings is described this way, from Latin for 'call out'.

parts.note: a bonehead's thinking has turned to bone, and the word describes being rigid and unthinking

explanation.surface: The word that best sums up a dimwit.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means turned to bone, and also stuck in rigid habits of thought, which suits a bonehead.
explanation.definitionFit: Tissue turned into bone, or a mind set rigid, is described this way, fitting a bonehead both ways.

parts.note: the rest is what remains, and a cryptic reading asks how many remain

explanation.surface: A question about what remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Rest' suggests what remains, but the answer says that nothing does.
explanation.definitionFit: Where the remainder is nothing, the phrase says nothing remains.

clue.text: Explain away the loss of lustre

definitions.meaning: to skim over a fault to hide it
read as 'the shine is finished', when the sheen has gone

explanation.definitionFit: To hide a fault with a quick excuse is to smooth it away; read as two words, it says the shine has ended.

indicators.note: turn tells us the word for about is read backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning
telling someone 'go!' dismisses them

explanation.surface: A drill sergeant barks 'About turn!' then 'Dismiss!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'About turn' sounds like a parade-ground order, but it turns RE into ER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for 'therefore' introduces a conclusion, just like 'and so'.

parts.note: the first witch says a sailor's wife's husband has sailed to a Syrian city, master of the Tiger

explanation.surface: A line from Macbeth with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Macbeth the witch names a city in Syria as the place the Tiger's master has sailed to.

clue.text: "Sit, --: look how the floor of heaven Is thick inlaid " (M. of v.)

definitions.text: "Sit, --: look how the floor of heaven Is thick inlaid " (M. of v.)

parts.words: "Sit, --: look how the floor of heaven Is thick inlaid " (M. of v.)
parts.note: Lorenzo says this to Shylock's daughter in The Merchant of Venice

explanation.surface: A line from The Merchant of Venice with a name missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorenzo addresses Shylock's daughter by name in this starry speech in The Merchant of Venice.

clue.text: Fair enough about love in the tournament

indicators.note: the word for fair goes around the love letter

parts.note: just means fair
love is zero in tennis, written as O

explanation.surface: A knight fair-mindedly courting during a tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: O (love, a nil score in tennis) sits inside JUST.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounted knights fighting with lances were the chief event of a medieval tournament.

definitions.meaning: Sir John Vanbrugh's Restoration comedy of 1696 bears this title

explanation.walkthrough: Vanbrugh's play was a sequel to Cibber's 'Love's Last Shift'.
explanation.definitionFit: Falling back into bad habits has this name, which is also the title of Vanbrugh's 1696 comedy.

clue.text: It's a bit stiff to dress, I would say

parts.note: to rig out is to dress
I'd is short for I would

explanation.surface: Someone thinks the dress code a little strict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' is a link that leads in to the abbreviation I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unbending and inflexible is stiff.

clue.text: Guilt is 'in an involved state, employing this

indicators.note: involved means tangled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Guilt is tangled up in what this person is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of GUILT IS IN gives the answer; the stray apostrophe is the printer's.
explanation.definitionFit: Making use of something is employing it.

parts.note: a small mischievous sprite, so 'a bit' hints at his small size

explanation.surface: Someone who is slightly naughty.
explanation.definitionFit: A little devil or naughty child is a small mischievous figure.

clue.text: Each runner starts with one, not only in selling plates

definitions.text: Each runner starts with one, not only in selling plates

parts.words: Each runner starts with one, not only in selling plates
parts.note: every horse in a race has a starting quote of odds, and in a selling plate the winner is also auctioned

explanation.surface: Every horse in a race carries some value, not just in races where it is sold.
explanation.walkthrough: A selling plate is a horse race after which the winner is auctioned, so price has two senses: betting odds and sale money.
explanation.definitionFit: Each horse has odds at the start, the starting price, and in a seller the horse also fetches a sum.

definitions.meaning: a valve that turns off water, or a bung

explanation.definitionFit: Dancing in metal-tipped shoes has this name, and so does a valve that stops the flow.

definitions.meaning: a thick woollen cloth used for coats had this name
split as dread and nought, it means fearing nothing

explanation.definitionFit: A heavy cloth for coats has this name, and split in two it means fear nothing.
